title: Prenatal care and the maternity record in Germany
intro: In Germany, antenatal care is provided by midwives and gynaecologists, and the costs of standard check-ups are covered by statutory health insurance. Your findings are recorded in a maternity record, often called the Mutterpass, which you carry with you. This article describes the usual arrangements; details can change, so check with your practice or insurer.

sections.heading: Who provides care
paragraphs: You can choose a gynaecologist, a midwife or both. Midwives can carry out many routine check-ups, and early contact with a midwife is recommended because places for after-birth home visits can fill up quickly. Many practices also offer information on birth locations such as hospitals, birth centres and home births.

sections.heading: Routine appointments
paragraphs: Check-ups usually take place every four weeks until the thirty-second week and then every two weeks. They include weighing, blood pressure, urine tests, measuring the womb and listening to the baby's heartbeat. Blood tests check blood group, anaemia and infections such as syphilis, with an offer of HIV testing. A blood sugar screening is usually offered between the twenty-fourth and twenty-eighth week.

sections.heading: Ultrasound examinations
paragraphs: Three routine ultrasound examinations are generally offered: around weeks nine to twelve, nineteen to twenty-two and twenty-nine to thirty-two. Additional examinations are used if there is a medical reason. Optional tests, such as detailed scans or blood tests for chromosomal conditions, may have conditions for coverage, so ask what applies.

sections.heading: The maternity record
paragraphs: The Mutterpass contains your medical history, test results, ultrasound data, blood group and risk factors, and notes of each visit. Carry it at all times, particularly when travelling and when going to hospital, so that any professional can see important information. Ask for explanations of any entries or abbreviations you do not understand.

sections.heading: Rights and support
paragraphs: Pregnant employees have protection at work, including maternity protection periods before and after birth and protection from dismissal. Counselling centres offer advice on benefits, finances and legal matters, and they are available also for people with limited German or uncertain residence status. Ask about interpreter services.

examples.title: Finding a midwife
examples.text: Imagine you have just learned you are pregnant. You could contact a midwife early, ask whether she offers home visits after the birth, and also book your first gynaecology visit.

examples.title: Travelling with your record
examples.text: Suppose you travel within Germany late in pregnancy. You might carry your Mutterpass and insurance card in your bag so that any emergency team can quickly see your information.
